openingLine: Hi! My doctor sent me over about my gallbladder. I feel fine right now, but these attacks are wrecking my evenings.

rounds.prompt: Morgan has told you why she is here. What do you do next?

choices.text: Tell her it is probably heartburn and suggest antacids
choices.feedback: Labeling the pain before taking a history misses the meal-triggered pattern that points to the gallbladder.
choices.patientCue: Honestly, I take Tums sometimes. But these attacks feel like something else, and I want them sorted out.

choices.text: Ask whether she smokes
choices.feedback: Social history can wait until the pattern of the main complaint is clear.
choices.patientCue: No, I don't smoke. Maybe a glass of wine a week. But, um, should I tell you about the attacks?

choices.text: Ask her to rate her pain right now from zero to ten
choices.feedback: Severity is worth knowing, but she is pain-free today, so the timing and triggers of the attacks tell you far more.
choices.patientCue: Right now, zero. During an attack, it's an eight.

choices.text: Ask when the attacks started, how many she has had, and what brings them on
choices.feedback: Four attacks in three months, each after a fatty dinner and settling in two to three hours, is the classic biliary pattern and justifies elective surgery.
choices.patientCue: Okay, so the first one was about three months ago, and I've had four. The last was eight days ago. It's always after a big or greasy dinner, and it eases off on its own after two or three hours.

rounds.prompt: Each attack follows a fatty dinner and settles within two to three hours. What do you do next?

choices.text: Reassure her the attacks will stop on their own and move on
choices.feedback: Dismissing recurrent attacks skips the questions that rule out complications like cholecystitis or a duct stone.
choices.patientCue: Here's the thing, I've had four of them now. I'd really like to get this sorted out.

choices.text: Ask what the pain feels like and where it spreads
choices.feedback: Steady pain under the right ribs going to the shoulder blade fits the gallbladder, but it does not screen for complications.
choices.patientCue: Up under my right ribs, sometimes in the middle under my breastbone, and sometimes through to my back near my right shoulder blade. It builds over about twenty minutes, then it's a hard, steady squeezing.

choices.text: Ask about fever or chills, dark urine, and pale or greasy stools
choices.feedback: No fever, dark urine or pale stools argues against cholecystitis, cholangitis and a stone blocking the bile duct.
choices.patientCue: No fevers or chills, not even during the attacks. My urine has never looked dark, and my bowels are normal. No pale or greasy stools, no blood.

choices.text: Ask whether anyone in her family has had heart disease
choices.feedback: Family cardiac history does not tell you whether she has a complicated gallstone problem right now.
choices.patientCue: Not that I know of. My mom had her gallbladder out in her forties, that's the main thing.

rounds.prompt: The attack story is clear. Before you plan anything, what do you do next?

choices.text: Ask about her medical conditions, every medicine she takes, and exactly what happened with penicillin
choices.feedback: Diabetes on metformin needs a perioperative glucose plan, and a childhood rash with later safe cephalexin means cefazolin is fine.
choices.patientCue: Type 2 diabetes, about five years, and high blood pressure. Metformin 500 twice a day with meals, lisinopril 10 in the morning, sometimes Tums. Penicillin gave me an itchy rash as a kid, no swelling or trouble breathing, and I've had cephalexin since with no problem.

choices.text: Confirm the penicillin allergy on the chart and ask if she has any others
choices.feedback: Confirming the label is a start, but without the reaction details and her medicine list you cannot choose the antibiotic or plan for her diabetes.
choices.patientCue: Yes, penicillin. That's the only one.

choices.text: Ask what she ate for lunch today
choices.feedback: Last meal matters on the day of surgery, not in clinic while her medicines and allergy are still unknown.
choices.patientCue: A salad at noon, before I came in. Is that a problem?

choices.text: Mark all cephalosporins as off limits because of the penicillin label
choices.feedback: An unexamined penicillin label pushes teams to broader, less effective antibiotics when cefazolin is safe for her.
choices.patientCue: Wait, I've had cephalexin since then with no problem. Is that the same kind of thing? Sorry, I just want to understand.

rounds.prompt: She is 38 and may need an operation and anesthesia. What do you do next?

choices.text: Ask about past operations and how anesthesia went
choices.feedback: Her C-section scar and uneventful anesthesia are useful, but pregnancy status matters more before elective surgery.
choices.patientCue: Just a C-section with my son, eight years ago. The anesthesia went fine.

choices.text: Ask whether her mother had gallbladder problems
choices.feedback: Family history is interesting but does not change whether elective anesthesia is safe for her today.
choices.patientCue: Yes, my mom had her gallbladder out in her forties. Honestly, I figured this might be like hers.

choices.text: Ask how much alcohol she drinks
choices.feedback: Her drinking is minimal and does not address the reproductive-age safety question.
choices.patientCue: Maybe a glass of wine a week. Not much at all.

choices.text: Ask about her last period and what contraception she uses
choices.feedback: Condom-only contraception in a 38-year-old means pregnancy must be excluded before elective surgery.
choices.patientCue: My last period started about three weeks ago, it was normal. We're not trying, but I'm not on birth control. We use condoms.

rounds.prompt: Time to examine her. What do you do next?

choices.text: Press deep at McBurney point in the right lower quadrant
choices.feedback: McBurney point tests for appendicitis, not the gallbladder.
choices.patientCue: Nope, nothing there.

finding.label: Right lower quadrant
finding.text: Nontender in the right lower quadrant.

choices.text: Palpate the abdomen, then press under the right ribs as she breathes in (Murphy sign)
choices.feedback: A soft abdomen and negative Murphy sign between attacks support uncomplicated gallstones rather than cholecystitis.
choices.patientCue: That's fine. Maybe a little sore up on the right, but nothing like an attack. And a little tender when I breathe in, but I can breathe in fine.

finding.label: Abdomen and Murphy sign
finding.text: Soft. Minimal right upper quadrant tenderness to deep palpation, no guarding, no mass. Negative Murphy sign between attacks.

choices.text: Check vital signs and general appearance
choices.feedback: Normal vitals and no jaundice fit colic, but the abdominal exam is what separates colic from cholecystitis.
choices.patientCue: Sure, go ahead.

finding.label: Vitals and appearance
finding.text: Temperature 36.8 C, heart rate 74, blood pressure 126/80, respiratory rate 14, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Weight 74 kg, BMI 27. Well appearing and comfortable. No jaundice or scleral icterus.

choices.text: Tap over her back for costovertebral angle tenderness
choices.feedback: CVA tenderness screens for kidney problems, which her history does not suggest.
choices.patientCue: No.

rounds.prompt: Her exam is benign today. Which workup do you order?

choices.text: CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast
choices.feedback: CT adds radiation and misses many gallstones; ultrasound is the test.
choices.patientCue: Okay, sure.

finding.label: CT abdomen and pelvis
finding.text: No acute abnormality. Gallstones not well seen on CT.

choices.text: Right upper quadrant ultrasound and liver tests
choices.feedback: This confirms stones and a normal duct but skips the pregnancy test and kidney and glucose check she needs before elective surgery.
choices.patientCue: Okay, sure. Do I need to be fasting? I had a salad at noon.

finding.label: Ultrasound and LFTs
finding.text: Ultrasound: Multiple mobile gallstones up to 12 mm. Gallbladder wall 2 mm, no pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy sign negative. Common bile duct 4 mm. Normal liver. LFTs: Total bilirubin 0.6, alkaline phosphatase 82, AST 22, ALT 25. Normal.

choices.text: Right upper quadrant ultrasound, liver tests, CBC, basic metabolic panel and a urine pregnancy test
choices.feedback: This confirms stones, rules out a duct stone and inflammation, checks kidney function and glucose for metformin, and excludes pregnancy.
choices.patientCue: Okay, sure. A pregnancy test makes sense, go ahead.

finding.label: Workup
finding.text: Ultrasound: Multiple mobile gallstones up to 12 mm. Gallbladder wall 2 mm, no pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy sign negative. Common bile duct 4 mm. Normal liver. LFTs: Total bilirubin 0.6, alkaline phosphatase 82, AST 22, ALT 25. Normal. CBC: White count 7.2, hemoglobin 13.5, platelets 260. Normal. BMP: Sodium 139, potassium 4.2, creatinine 0.86, glucose 118. Normal kidney function. Pregnancy test: Urine hCG negative.

choices.text: Send a lipase and stop there
choices.feedback: Lipase screens for pancreatitis, which she does not have, and it never shows the stones.
choices.patientCue: Okay, sure.

rounds.prompt: Pulling it all together, what is your diagnosis?

choices.text: Acute cholecystitis
choices.feedback: Attacks lasting two to three hours, no fever, a negative Murphy sign, normal white count and a 2 mm wall exclude cholecystitis.
choices.patientCue: Sorry, what does that mean? Is that the gallbladder thing?

choices.text: Choledocholithiasis
choices.feedback: Normal liver tests, a 4 mm duct and no dark urine or pale stools make a bile duct stone unlikely.
choices.patientCue: Okay, in English? I don't know that word.

choices.text: Gallstones
choices.feedback: Stones are present, but naming the symptomatic pattern, biliary colic, is what justifies removing the gallbladder.
choices.patientCue: Okay. So something's off with my gallbladder, like my mom?

choices.text: Symptomatic cholelithiasis (biliary colic)
choices.feedback: Recurrent steady pain after fatty meals that settles within hours, with stones on ultrasound and no inflammation, is biliary colic.
choices.patientCue: Sorry, what does that mean? So it's my gallbladder causing these attacks?

choices.text: Recommend elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy, holding metformin and lisinopril the morning of surgery
choices.feedback: Four attacks in three months with uncomplicated stones warrant elective keyhole gallbladder removal with a clear medication plan.
choices.patientCue: Honestly, good. I just want my evenings back. So when could we do it, and how long would I be off work?

choices.text: Admit her today for urgent laparoscopic cholecystectomy tomorrow
choices.feedback: Right operation, but she is pain-free with normal labs, so urgent admission is unnecessary.
choices.patientCue: Tomorrow? Okay, but I feel fine right now. I have a sub for today, but I didn't plan on staying.

choices.text: Refer her for ERCP to clear the bile duct first
choices.feedback: Normal liver tests and a 4 mm duct put her at low risk for a duct stone, so ERCP adds risk without benefit.
choices.patientCue: Sorry, what does that mean? Is that the same as taking care of the gallbladder?

choices.text: Advise a low-fat diet and follow up in six months, no surgery
choices.feedback: Symptomatic stones keep causing attacks and can lead to cholecystitis or pancreatitis, so diet alone is not enough.
choices.patientCue: Here's the thing, I've already been avoiding fatty food. I really just want these attacks sorted out.

closingLine: Honestly, good. I just want my evenings back. Okay, so when can we do it, how long will I be off work, and what can I eat afterward?
